introduction-wiring-vs-directory.core: Traditional service connectivity is wiring: peering, Transit Gateway, routes, security groups and load balancers between networks. VPC Lattice is a directory approach: services register once, consumers discover them by name, and Lattice handles routing, load balancing and auth across VPCs and accounts at layer 7, independent of network topology.

first_principles.problem: Connecting 80 microservices across 30 accounts requires a maze of routes, peering and internal load balancers.
truths: Services care about names, not routes.
Auth should be per service request.

analogy.title: A phone directory versus running cables between houses
analogy.story: Instead of wiring every house to every other, everyone looks up numbers in one directory.
analogy.breaks: Phone directories don't enforce who can call; Lattice auth policies do.

example.title: Before and after
flow: Before: TGW + 30 route tables + internal ALBs
After: services registered, consumer VPCs associated
Calls by DNS name with IAM auth

check.q: What does VPC Lattice abstract away?
check.a: Network-level wiring like peering, routes and internal load balancers between VPCs.

the-core-hierarchy.core: Lattice objects: a service network (logical boundary consumers associate with), services (with listeners and rules routing by path, header or method), target groups (instances, IPs, Lambda, ALB, ECS/EKS via controller) and associations linking VPCs and services to the network. Auth policies attach at network and service levels.

first_principles.problem: Teams can't see how requests get from a consumer VPC to a target behind a Lattice service.
derivation: **Associate** service and consumer VPCs to the network.

analogy.title: A shopping mall
analogy.story: The mall (service network), shops (services), staff behind counters (targets), and doors connecting car parks (VPC associations).
analogy.breaks: Malls have one owner; Lattice services can belong to different accounts.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Mixed compute behind one service name.

check.q: What do consumers associate their VPC with in Lattice?

the-killer-feature-overlapping-ips.core: Because Lattice uses a link-local data path and proxies requests at layer 7, consumer and provider VPCs can have overlapping CIDRs. No routes between VPCs are needed, which solves a classic blocker after acquisitions or when teams independently chose 10.0.0.0/16.

first_principles.problem: After an acquisition, both companies use 10.0.0.0/16 and can't peer or route between VPCs.
derivation: Use **Lattice** to connect services without routing.

analogy.title: A receptionist relaying messages between two buildings with identical room numbers
analogy.story: Room 101 exists in both, but the receptionist knows which building each message is for.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists relay any message; Lattice handles HTTP/gRPC (and TCP via resource configurations), not arbitrary protocols everywhere.

example.title: Post-acquisition integration
flow: Acquired company's billing service registered in Lattice
Parent VPC associated with service network

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Integration in days, not a re-IP project.

check.q: Why can Lattice connect VPCs with overlapping CIDRs?
check.a: It proxies requests at the application layer rather than routing packets between the networks.

zero-trust-iam-auth-policies.core: Lattice auth policies are IAM resource policies on service networks and services. With auth type AWS_IAM, callers sign requests with SigV4, and policies allow or deny by principal, org, tags, path or method. That's zero-trust per request: network location grants nothing, and identity does.

first_principles.problem: Any workload inside the VPC can call the payments API because security groups only check IPs.

analogy.title: Checking every visitor's badge at each office door
analogy.story: Being inside the building doesn't get you into the finance office.
analogy.breaks: Badge checks slow visitors; SigV4 signing adds minimal latency.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only checkout can POST to payments.

check.q: What must clients do when a Lattice service uses AWS_IAM auth?
check.a: Sign their requests with SigV4 using IAM credentials.

lattice-vs-alternatives-when-to-use-what.core: Use VPC Lattice for HTTP/gRPC service-to-service communication across many VPCs and accounts with IAM auth and no network plumbing. Use Transit Gateway for broad network-level connectivity (any protocol, on-prem). Use PrivateLink to expose a single service to many consumers. Use a service mesh (App Mesh successors, Istio) for in-cluster traffic policies and mTLS.

first_principles.problem: A team replaces Transit Gateway with Lattice and discovers its databases and on-prem systems still need network routing.
truths: Lattice operates at the application layer.

analogy.title: Postal services versus roads
analogy.story: Lattice delivers named parcels to the right office; roads let any vehicle go anywhere.
analogy.breaks: You can't drive a parcel service on its own; Lattice still runs over AWS networking underneath.

example.title: Hybrid estate
example.outcome: the right connectivity per use case.

check.q: When is Transit Gateway still needed alongside Lattice?
check.a: For network-level connectivity: non-HTTP protocols, broad VPC-to-VPC routing and on-prem/hybrid links.
